---
title: Nested context and account outcomes
description: "Nest line items inside transactions, add a withdrawal history, and predict an account-level loss beside transaction disputes."
engine: markdown
---

The [repeat-payment example](profile-context-and-a-second-outcome.qmd) predicts
two outcomes for each transaction in an account history. An account review team
also needs to know how much loss to expect across the account over the next month.

Keep the transaction sequence, including the latest payment once, and add
more account context. Purchases now have their own line items; cash withdrawals
form another event history with different fields. This advanced example
combines nested context, transaction predictions, and an account-level
target.

## One observation

```yaml
account_id: account-42
account_age_days: 420
trxns:
  - booked_at: "2026-03-28T09:00:00"
    amount: 24.00
    merchant: Harbor Internet
    channel: direct_debit
    line_items:
      - sku: internet-plan
        quantity: 1
    disputed: false
  - booked_at: "2026-04-28T09:00:00"
    amount: 24.00
    merchant: Harbor Internet
    channel: direct_debit
    line_items:
      - sku: internet-plan
        quantity: 1
    disputed: false
  - booked_at: "2026-05-27T08:00:00"
    amount: 32.00
    merchant: Station Cafe
    channel: card
    line_items:
      - sku: lunch
        quantity: 2
    disputed: true
  - booked_at: "2026-05-28T09:00:00"
    amount: 24.00
    merchant: Harbor Internet
    channel: direct_debit
    line_items:
      - sku: internet-plan
        quantity: 1
    disputed: false
recent_cash_withdrawals:
  - booked_at: "2026-05-26T16:00:00"
    amount: 100.00
    atm_region: home_region
loss_next_30_days: 0.0
```

One record describes an account at a decision time. Profile attributes,
transactions, line items, and withdrawals contain only information available
then. Purchase baskets can distinguish activity at the same merchant; cash
withdrawals provide another view of account behavior without inventing a
merchant or line items for an ATM event.

The cutoff is the final booking on May 28 at 09:00, following
[Prepare observations](prepare-observations.qmd). Each `disputed`
label covers the 30 days after it, and `loss_next_30_days` records total
account loss in the application's currency over the same window.

## Place each target with its subject

```python
import relflow as rf

model = rf.Model.md(
    account_age_days=rf.Number,
    trxns=rf.Branch(
        length=64,
        overflow="tail",
        booked_at=rf.DateParts(
            dateparts=["day_of_month", "day_of_week", "hour_of_day"],
        ),
        amount=rf.Number,
        merchant=rf.Category,
        channel=rf.Enum(values=("card", "direct_debit", "bank_transfer")),
        line_items=rf.Branch(
            length=16,
            sku=rf.Category,
            quantity=rf.Number,
        ),
        disputed=rf.Boolean(mask=True),
    ),
    recent_cash_withdrawals=rf.Branch(
        length=16,
        overflow="tail",
        booked_at=rf.DateParts(
            dateparts=["day_of_month", "day_of_week", "hour_of_day"],
        ),
        amount=rf.Number,
        atm_region=rf.Category,
    ),
    loss_next_30_days=rf.Number(mask=True),
)
```

Line items form context within each transaction. The transaction sequence then
sends its reduced representation to the account root, alongside the withdrawal
history. The dispute decoder uses its ancestor context and aligned visible
siblings; its output retains the
transaction coordinates. See [Model tree](../concepts/model-tree.qmd).

Both targets use `mask=True`. Every transaction's dispute label and the
account-loss label supply supervision while staying out of the inputs.

At prediction time, omit `loss_next_30_days` and omit `disputed` from every
transaction. Keep the transaction, line-item, and withdrawal records known
at the decision time; they define the positions and context to predict.

## Preserve the context the task needs

The `md` preset uses Attention reductions with four summaries per parent
coordinate. Those summaries bound the context sent upward; they are not one
token per original line item. If matching a SKU across transactions matters,
represent the shared relationship through aligned input or preprocessing.
Nesting does not join database tables.

`overflow="tail"` assumes transactions are sorted oldest to newest. The line
items keep the default first-items policy. Withdrawals are also oldest to
newest and retain their own last 16 records. The two histories have independent
lengths; matching list positions do not imply related events. Choose each
capacity from the records the application needs to model.

Fit the same way as earlier examples, using files prepared for this richer
account schema:

```python
data = rf.ArrowDataModule(
    train="accounts/risk/train.parquet",
    validate="accounts/risk/validation.parquet",
)
model.fit(data, batch_size=128, max_epochs=30)
```

## Evaluate the two outcomes

Fit using [data modules](../guides/data-modules.qmd) and
[Training options](../guides/training-options.qmd). Hold out later decision
windows and control overlap between related account snapshots.

Compare the transaction-only model, the addition of line items, and the
addition of withdrawals before attributing value to the complete schema.
Inspect dispute ranking and calibration separately from account-loss errors.
Their combined validation loss can hide a regression in one target. This
example specifies a model design; it makes no claim about measured quality.

Every transaction's dispute result is at `predictions.trxns[i].disputed`,
and the account loss is `predictions.loss_next_30_days`.
All retained dispute positions have `inferred: true`. Retain `account_id` and the
application's transaction identifiers when joining outputs back to records.
Account for the retained history window: an attention summary is not a
transaction identifier.
See [Prediction output](../reference/prediction-output.qmd).

Next, when labels are scarce,
[pretrain](pretraining-and-fine-tuning.qmd) on the observed transaction fields
before adapting the model to an outcome. That guide changes the learning
objective while keeping the payment-history modeling pattern.
